title: Identify Responsibility Split Between AGV Onboard Sensors, Geek+ RMS, and WCS for Routing and Alarm Codes
summary: Use this checklist to map the responsibility for obstacle sensing, alarm code generation/visibility, task queuing/execution, and routing decision across Geek+ AGV onboard hardware, Geek+ RMS, and WCS/office software—using only the responsibility split described in the provided training segment.
when_to_use: When you need to explain or confirm, for a given observed behavior, which component owns that responsibility in the Geek+ AGV / Geek+ RMS / WCS architecture described in the segment (obstacle sensing, alarm code visibility, task queuing/execution, and routing decision).
not_for: Do not use this procedure to perform live troubleshooting of specific faults (e.g., specific AGV fault codes, tipper faults, or queue states) because it does not provide system-specific diagnostic steps beyond mapping responsibilities.
roles_and_responsibilities: L1_support: Use the checklist to map observed behaviors to the responsibility owners (AGV sensors vs RMS vs WCS) exactly as described in the segment.
access_or_tools_needed: RMS screen visibility (as referenced in the segment)

visual_references.description: Segment frame showing the responsibility split: AGVs operate over QR codes, directly controlled by Geek+ RMS; Geek+ handles movement and determines best route; includes forward collision sensors and fenced operation context.

steps.title: Confirm the control architecture described in the segment (AGVs over QR codes; controlled by Geek+ RMS)
steps.purpose: Establish the baseline ownership model so later mapping of obstacle/alarm/task/routing behaviors is consistent.
steps.instruction: State the segment’s architecture: the AGVs operate over QR codes and are controlled by the Geek+ RMS (Geek+ RMS is the robot management software that dictates what the robot needs to do).
steps.expected_result: You can clearly state that, in this architecture, Geek+ RMS is the robot management layer controlling AGV movement over QR-code operation.
steps.healthy_condition: Your mapping consistently treats Geek+ RMS as the controller for movement execution and routing decision (not the AGV hardware and not WCS).
steps.failure_condition: You cannot consistently explain which component is responsible for movement control and routing decision as described in the segment.

actions.label: Map architecture ownership
actions.exact_action: Use the segment’s language: “They operate over QR codes” and “They are controlled by the Geek Plus RMS… Geek Plus handles all movements.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot clearly state the segment’s control architecture ownership (AGV QR-code operation + Geek+ RMS control), stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript: “They operate over QR codes. They are controlled by the Geek Plus RMS… Geek Plus handles all movements… communicate directly with the Agvs.”
Segment frame includes: “Operate over QR codes” and “Directly controlled by Geek+ RMS.”

steps.title: For obstacle detection: identify that AGV onboard physical/collision sensors detect an obstacle and report the condition back to RMS
steps.purpose: Assign obstacle sensing responsibility to the correct component (AGV hardware vs RMS vs WCS).
steps.instruction: State that obstacle detection is performed by the AGV onboard physical/collision sensors, which trigger when an obstacle is present and report the information back to RMS.
steps.expected_result: You can map “obstacle detected” behavior to AGV onboard sensors reporting back to RMS.
steps.healthy_condition: Your explanation includes that the physical hardware triggers “Hey, I have an obstacle in front of me” and sends that information to RMS.
steps.failure_condition: You attribute obstacle sensing to RMS or WCS rather than to the AGV onboard sensors as described in the segment.

actions.label: Map obstacle sensing ownership
actions.exact_action: Use the segment’s language: “Inside AGV you have the sensors… collision sensors… it takes all those information and sends it back to RMS… physical hardware itself will trigger… obstacle… reports back to RMS.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot map obstacle detection to AGV onboard sensors reporting to RMS, stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript: “Inside AGV you have the sensors… collision sensors… sends it back to RMS… physical hardware itself will trigger… obstacle… reports back to RMS.”
Segment frame includes “These AGVs have forward collision sensors”.

steps.title: For alarm visibility: verify that RMS generates an alarm code visible on the RMS screen
steps.purpose: Assign alarm-code generation and visibility to RMS (not AGV hardware and not WCS).
steps.instruction: State that when the AGV reports an obstacle condition to RMS, RMS generates an alarm code that is visible to users on the RMS screen (including “UPS whoever’s looking at the RMS screen”).
steps.expected_result: You can map “alarm code shown on RMS screen” behavior to RMS generating the alarm code after receiving obstacle information from the AGV.
steps.healthy_condition: Your explanation includes that RMS generates an alarm code visible on the RMS screen.
steps.failure_condition: You cannot explain where the alarm code is generated or you attribute alarm-code generation to the AGV or WCS.

actions.label: Map alarm-code ownership
actions.exact_action: Use the segment’s language: “RMS generates a alarm code which is visible… on the RMS screen.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot map alarm visibility to RMS generating an alarm code visible on the RMS screen, stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript: “It reports back to RMS, RMS generates a alarm code which is visible to us and UPS whoever's looking at the RMS screen.”
Segment frame supports the RMS role as robot management system controlling movement and reporting/visibility context.

steps.title: For task assignment and queuing: identify that WCS assigns tasks and they queue in RMS
steps.purpose: Assign task assignment/queuing responsibility to WCS (assignment) and RMS (queue ownership).
steps.instruction: State that WCS/office software assigns robot movement tasks (move from location to location, then to the next), and those tasks go into a queue that lives in RMS.
steps.expected_result: You can map “movement task assigned” to WCS assignment and “task queue exists” to RMS queue ownership.
steps.healthy_condition: Your explanation includes that tasks assigned by WCS go into a queue which lives in RMS.
steps.failure_condition: You attribute task queuing to WCS or task assignment to RMS rather than WCS as described in the segment.

actions.label: Map task assignment/queue ownership
actions.exact_action: Use the segment’s language: “All the task that is assigned by… WCS… goes in a queue which lives in RMS.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot map task assignment to WCS and task queuing to RMS, stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript: “All the task that is assigned by… WCS… a robot needs to move… So all those tiles, it goes in a queue which lives in RMS.”
Segment frame context: RMS is the robot management system controlling movement execution.

steps.title: For execution: confirm that RMS executes tasks 1 by 1 by sending commands to the AGV; AGV has no knowledge of the task queue
steps.purpose: Assign task execution responsibility to RMS and clarify that the AGV only knows what is happening (not the queue logic).
steps.instruction: State that RMS executes queued tasks 1 by 1 by sending commands to the AGV, and that the AGV does not have knowledge of the task queue.
steps.expected_result: You can map “sequential task execution” to RMS sending commands to the AGV, with AGV lacking queue knowledge.
steps.healthy_condition: Your explanation includes: “RMS executes those tasks 1 by 1 by sending the command to the AGV” and “AGB doesn’t have knowledge… AGB only knows what's happening.”
steps.failure_condition: You claim the AGV maintains/understands the task queue or that WCS directly executes tasks on the AGV.

actions.label: Map execution ownership
actions.exact_action: Use the segment’s language: “RMS executes those tasks 1 by 1 by sending the command to the AGB… AGB doesn't have knowledge… AGB only knows what's happening.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot map task execution to RMS sending commands to the AGV (and AGV lacking queue knowledge), stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript: “RMS executes those tasks 1 by 1 by sending the command to the AGB… AGB doesn't have knowledge… AGB only knows what's happening.”

steps.title: For routing: confirm that routing is decided by RMS (Geek+ determines the best route from point A to point B)
steps.purpose: Assign routing decision responsibility to RMS/Geek+ (not AGV hardware and not WCS).
steps.instruction: State that routing is decided by RMS, and that Geek+ determines the best route to navigate from point A to point B.
steps.expected_result: You can map “route choice” behavior to RMS routing decision (Geek+ determines best route).
steps.healthy_condition: Your explanation includes: “So the routing is decided by RMS” and “Geek+ determines the best route to navigate from point A to point B.”
steps.failure_condition: You attribute routing decision to the AGV or to WCS rather than RMS as described in the segment.

actions.label: Map routing ownership
actions.exact_action: Use the segment’s language: “So the routing is decided by RMS… The routing is decided by RMS… Geek+ determines the best route to navigate from point A to point B.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot map routing decision to RMS/Geek+ as described in the segment, stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript: “So the routing is decided by RMS… The routing is decided by RMS.”
Segment frame includes: “Geek+ determines the best route to navigate from point A to point B.”

steps.title: Stop when you can clearly state the component owner for each responsibility (AGV sensors, RMS alarm codes/execution, WCS task assignment, RMS routing)
steps.purpose: Provide a clear completion gate aligned to the candidate’s expected result.
steps.instruction: Using only the segment’s described language, confirm you can map each observed behavior to its responsibility owner: obstacle sensing (AGV), alarm code generation/visibility (RMS), task queuing/execution (RMS), and routing decision (RMS), with task assignment originating from WCS.
steps.expected_result: You can produce a complete mapping statement that assigns each responsibility to exactly one owner as described in the segment.
steps.healthy_condition: Your mapping covers all four areas (obstacle sensing, alarm codes, task queuing/execution, routing) and includes WCS as the task assignment origin.
steps.failure_condition: Any responsibility cannot be mapped to AGV vs RMS vs WCS using the segment’s described ownership model.

actions.label: Complete mapping check
actions.exact_action: Perform a final checklist-style verbal mapping: “AGV sensors report to RMS; RMS generates alarm codes and executes queued tasks; WCS assigns tasks; RMS decides routing.”

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot map a behavior to one of the described responsibility owners (AGV vs RMS vs WCS), stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Transcript contains the full mapping: AGV sensors report to RMS; RMS generates alarm code visible on RMS screen; WCS assigns tasks that queue in RMS; RMS executes tasks 1 by 1 by sending commands to the AGV; routing decided by RMS.

success_criteria: You can map obstacle detection to AGV onboard sensors reporting to RMS.
You can map alarm code visibility on the RMS screen to RMS generating the alarm code.
You can map task assignment origin to WCS and task queuing/execution to RMS (queue lives in RMS; RMS executes tasks 1 by 1 by sending commands to the AGV).
You can map routing decision to RMS/Geek+ (best route from point A to point B).
healthy_conditions: Your ownership mapping consistently treats RMS as the robot management system controlling movement execution and routing decision.
Your ownership mapping consistently treats the AGV as having sensors/collision sensing and reporting to RMS, without queue knowledge.
failure_conditions: You cannot assign any of the responsibilities (obstacle sensing, alarm code generation/visibility, task queuing/execution, routing decision) to the correct component owner as described in the segment.
escalation_guidance: If you cannot map a behavior to one of the described responsibility owners (AGV vs RMS vs WCS), stop and escalate for system-specific clarification beyond what this segment provides.
